prize_parts.citation: for incorporating firm heterogeneity into trade theory, and for showing how selection and reallocation across firms shape exporting, multinational activity and the gains from trade

statement.case_for: B010 is still my first choice after reading the openings. It is a single, well-defined discovery. Melitz (2003) moved trade analysis from industries to firms. Selection into exporting, within-industry reallocation and a new channel for gains from trade followed from that move. Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple on exports versus FDI, and Helpman's earlier trade theory, extend the idea into multinational organisation and firm boundaries. The framework is more than two decades old and is standard in teaching, empirical work and policy evaluation. It also links micro-level productivity differences to aggregate welfare, which is a core concern of dynamic macro and growth economics. The openings show unusually broad agreement that the Helpman-Melitz pairing is the right credit assignment, with Redding treated as a later extension. I take that as a convergence of independent attribution judgments, not as evidence of merit. I would keep the citation to the firm-heterogeneity discovery and not turn it into a lifetime-achievement citation for Helpman.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is credit. Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum, and Eaton-Kortum, are important precursors and parallel contributors who are not on the ballot, so a Helpman-Melitz award would leave out people with real claims to the empirical and quantitative strands. A second reservation is that parts of the quantitative gains-from-trade results depend on parametric assumptions such as Pareto productivity draws. A third is field balance, since trade was recognised in 2008 for new trade theory. I think the heterogeneous-firm contribution is distinct from that earlier recognition, but the committee should test the claim and not assume it.

responses.point: Boppart ranked B010 sixth. He asks whether it is a separate advance beyond the new trade theory honoured in 2008, and whether Redding or the Bernard-Jensen exporter-facts work belongs in the credit.
responses.response: The distinctness question is the right one. My answer is that new trade theory explained intra-industry trade and scale with representative firms. Melitz and Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple explain which firms export or invest abroad, why aggregate productivity changes after liberalisation, and how reallocation produces welfare gains. Those are different mechanisms with different testable predictions, and the firm-level evidence has confirmed many of them. I agree with Boppart that Bernard-Jensen deserve recognition for the exporter facts. But those facts motivated the theory and did not supply the unifying model. I would keep Redding out of the core because his main contribution is quantitative and spatial trade, which builds on this base.

responses.point: Krusell ranks B037 first. He sees the New Keynesian framework as the working core of monetary policy analysis, and he defends a Calvo-Taylor-Woodford triad as foundational pricing, policy rule and integrated framework.
responses.response: I agree on influence. I ranked B037 sixth, not lower, for that reason. My difficulty is attribution, which several openings (Boppart, Enflo, Stromberg, Hjalmarsson) also raise. Gali, Gertler, Christiano, Eichenbaum, Smets, Clarida and Rotemberg each have strong claims, so any three-name cut leaves out major contributors. The post-2021 inflation episode also left open how well the baseline model performs. I do not think a clean citation yet exists for B037. If the committee can find a defensible boundary, I would reconsider. At the moment B010 and B003 have clearer credit lines.

responses.point: Teorell, Boppart, Dreber, Krusell, Stromberg and Andersson want B019 limited to Kiyotaki and Moore. They treat 1997 as the clear origin of the collateral-constraint mechanism, and they see the financial-accelerator strand as overlapping with the 2022 recognition of Bernanke.
responses.response: This qualifies my opening, where I included Gertler. I now think the two-name attribution is the more defensible one. Kiyotaki-Moore is a distinct, identifiable mechanism. The accelerator literature, including Bernanke-Gertler-Gilchrist, adds credit lines that interact with the 2022 prize and with Gertler's presence on B037. If B019 is pursued, I would support Kiyotaki and Moore as the core. I would not call the Gertler question settled, since his later work with Kiyotaki on intermediation is substantive. I keep B019 as an alternative and not as my preferred configuration because I rank B010 higher on breadth of influence and clarity of the citation.

responses.point: Andersson ranks B003 first. The BLP core of Berry, Levinsohn and Pakes is clearly identifiable, the methods are standard in antitrust and regulation, and Bresnahan, Reiss, Benkard and Levin raise a boundary question.
responses.response: I agree that the BLP trio is the cleanest credit structure on any empirical-methods ballot. I ranked B003 second for that reason. The question for me is whether the committee should frame it as a methods award or as a substantive discovery about market power and welfare. Bresnahan's earlier empirical IO work is also a legitimate omission to worry about, and I do not think the three-name limit settles it. I keep B003 as my strongest alternative. I do not put it first because B010 has a more unified conceptual advance.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will require credit for Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum, or for Redding, alongside Helpman and Melitz.
Whether the quantitative gains-from-trade results, which depend on parametric assumptions, weaken the case for the core discovery.
Whether B003 should include Bresnahan, and whether the committee prefers a methods-oriented award in IO.
Whether the B019 attribution should include Gertler, given the overlap with the 2022 prize and his appearance on B037.
My assessments rely on my own recollection of the literature and have not been independently verified against sources.
statement.conflict_note: No connection to the shortlisted candidates is apparent from the supplied profile, and none of the candidates listed for B010, B003 or B019 appears among his documented co-authors or institutional ties. He discloses collegial ties to committee members: IIES colleague of Krusell and Boppart, co-author with Boppart and Friberg, and a frequent co-author of Krusell. These ties are disclosed and not adjudicated. His own climate-economics and macro-public-finance work is not part of the shortlist.
